summary: Outlines standard mechanisms that help TCP use the available capacity of network paths that include satellite links. These links have long delays, so extra care is needed. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: A satellite link makes messages take a long time to reach you, like talking to someone on the moon. This lists tricks to keep TCP efficient.

questions: how to improve tcp over satellite links
why is tcp slow over satellite
why do large tcp windows matter on satellite links
subtitle: Standard TCP and link-level mechanisms that help TCP fill long, high-delay satellite paths.

tldr.problem: Satellite links add long delay, noise, asymmetric capacity and sometimes changing delay, so ordinary TCP uses little of the available capacity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends Path MTU Discovery and forward error correction below TCP, and standard TCP features: slow start and congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery, large windows with PAWS and RTTM, and selective acknowledgments.
tldr.outcome: Every mitigation is an IETF standards track mechanism or compliant with one, and Table 1 sorts them into Recommended and Required for satellite networks.

today: RFC 2488 is a Best Current Practice, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its advice reflects the TCP standards cited in 1999, such as RFC 2001 and RFC 1323.

sections.title: Scope and Approach
sections.content:
Satellite channel characteristics can change how transport protocols such as TCP (RFC 793) behave, and poor behavior means low channel utilization. Other things matter too, such as the data link protocol, application protocol, router buffer size, queueing discipline and proxy location, but this document focuses on TCP.

Many mitigations have been proposed by researchers. This RFC considers only mechanisms that are currently well understood and on the IETF standards track (or compliant with IETF standards). Section 3 covers two non-TCP mechanisms, Section 4 the TCP mechanisms, and Section 5 a summary of what a satellite friendly TCP should include.
sections.plainLanguage: This note only suggests tricks that are already well tested and approved, not brand new experiments.

sections.title: How Satellite Links Behave
sections.content:
A message over a satellite link is delayed by the speed of light and the satellite's altitude. A geostationary (GSO) satellite sits at approximately 36,000 km. The one-hop propagation time is 239.6 ms for a ground station directly below the satellite and 279.0 ms at the edge of the view area, so a round-trip time (RTT) could be at least 558 ms. Other links, queueing and on-board processing add more. Low Earth Orbit (LEO) delays range from several milliseconds to as much as 80 ms.

Two basic limits apply. Noise: signals weaken with distance, and typical bit error rates are on the order of 1 error per 10 million bits (1 x 10^-7) or less frequent. Bandwidth: the radio spectrum is limited and usually controlled by licenses.

The RFC lists the characteristics that can hurt TCP:

  • Long feedback loop: it takes a long time to learn whether a packet arrived.
  • Large delay*bandwidth product: TCP must keep a large amount of data in flight to fill the channel.
  • Transmission errors: TCP treats every drop as congestion and shrinks its window, even when corruption caused it.
  • Asymmetric use: for example, a slow dialup return path with a satellite downlink.
  • Variable round trip times: for example in LEO constellations; whether this affects TCP is called an open question.
  • Intermittent connectivity: handoffs in non-GSO configurations may cause packet loss.

Most satellite channels show only some of these, and the mechanisms should also help other networks, such as gigabit networks with large delay*bandwidth products.
sections.plainLanguage: Signals going up to a satellite and back take a long time, and the radio signal can get fuzzy. TCP has to be patient and keep lots of messages in flight so the line stays busy.

sections.title: Lower Level Mitigations
sections.content:
Two non-TCP mechanisms are recommended for satellite networks. The data link protocol also matters: its flow control window should not be too small, and how link level retransmissions interact with TCP retransmissions is called a subject for further research.

Path MTU Discovery finds the largest packet size usable on a path without IP fragmentation. The sender sets the IP don't fragment (DF) bit, and a gateway that cannot forward the packet returns an ICMP message with the largest size it can forward. Larger packets carry more data per overhead byte and let the congestion window, which grows in segments, grow faster in bytes. The drawback is a possible delay before data flows, which satellite delay can worsen, though the RFC says in practice discovery does not take long because common MTU values are widely supported. Its use is recommended.

Forward error correction (FEC) improves the bit error rate. TCP treats every loss as congestion and takes a long time to recover over a satellite link, so the link should be made as clean as possible. The RFC makes no specific BER recommendation other than that it should be as low as possible. FEC is not a cure-all: it does not solve military jamming, deep space missions or rain fade, and it needs extra hardware, uses some bandwidth and can add delay and jitter. Detecting corruption loss is still a research issue, and wrongly assuming loss is not congestion can lead to congestive collapse.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the biggest envelopes the road allows, and use a spell-checker style code so garbled messages get fixed on the way instead of making TCP slow down.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Loss Recovery
sections.content:
TCP uses four congestion control algorithms: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery. They rely on two variables: the congestion window (cwnd), an upper bound on data in flight limited by the receiver's advertised window, and the slow start threshold (ssthresh), which selects the algorithm used to grow cwnd.

In slow start, cwnd starts at 1 segment and grows by 1 segment per ACK. In congestion avoidance, cwnd grows by 1/cwnd per ACK, roughly 1 segment per RTT. After the first segment, a GSO sender idles for roughly 500 ms, so these phases take more real time over satellites. This is why larger packets from Path MTU Discovery matter.

On a retransmission timeout, ssthresh becomes half of cwnd and cwnd drops to 1 segment. With fast retransmit, 3 duplicate ACKs cause the missing segment to be resent without waiting for the timeout. Fast recovery then sets ssthresh to half of cwnd, halves cwnd, and inflates it by 1 segment per duplicate ACK. Fast retransmit generally resends only one segment per window, so multiple losses in a window usually wait for the timeout and fall back to slow start.

These algorithms waste bandwidth on long-delay links, but they are needed to prevent congestive collapse in a shared network, so the benefit to the whole network outweighs the cost to one connection. Implementers are advised to follow RFC 2001 or subsequent versions.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP starts by sending just one message and doubles up as replies come back. If something is lost it slows down. On a satellite each wait is long, but this care keeps the shared road from jamming.

sections.title: Large Windows, ACKs and SACK
sections.content:
Large windows. The standard maximum TCP window of 65,535 bytes limits throughput to window size divided by RTT. With a GSO RTT of 560 ms that is 117,027 bytes/second, which cannot fill a T1 rate channel (approximately 192,000 bytes/second). The window scaling options of RFC 1323 should be used, along with the companion algorithms PAWS (Protection Against Wrapped Sequence space) and RTTM (Round-Trip Time Measurements). On a link shared by many flows large windows may not be needed: two connections with 65,535 byte windows can fully use a T1 GSO channel.

Acknowledgment strategies. Delayed ACKs, which RFC 1122 says hosts SHOULD use, produce an ACK for every second full-sized segment or after a timeout that must not exceed 500 ms. Because cwnd grows per ACK, growth is slower with delayed ACKs. Turning them off is not recommended, since doubling the number of ACKs in a shared network may have consequences not yet understood, so receivers should keep generating them.

Selective acknowledgments. SACKs (RFC 2018) tell the sender exactly which packets arrived. With SACK the sender can usually work out what to retransmit within the first RTT after loss detection, keeps the ACK clock running, and avoids a slow start period after multiple losses. The RFC calls a SACK based loss recovery algorithm the best way to improve fast retransmit and fast recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: A bigger bucket lets TCP keep more water in the pipe at once. Telling the sender exactly which pieces went missing means it only resends those pieces.

sections.title: Mitigation Summary
sections.content:
Table 1 lists each mechanism, whether it is Recommended or Required, the section that discusses it, and where it is implemented: S for the data sender, R for the data receiver and L for the satellite link. Required means the IETF defined it as required for hosts using the shared Internet (RFC 1122); Recommended means the authors recommend it for networks with satellite channels.

Satellite users are advised to check with TCP vendors that these mechanisms are supported in their stack. The RFC also names a planned memo on research into improving TCP over satellite channels, together with other considerations such as satellite network architectures.
sections.plainLanguage: The note ends with a checklist of which tricks are must-haves and which are strongly suggested, and who has to do each one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The authors believe the recommendations do not alter the security implications of TCP. A broadcast medium such as a satellite link does carry its own implications. Eavesdropping is a passive attack that could reveal traffic control information or compromise user data privacy, and because satellite signals can be received without a physical connection, monitoring can go undetected, although the resources needed to monitor a satellite link are non-trivial.

Encryption at the physical or link layer can secure the satellite hop, but traffic remains exposed before and after it, so end-to-end security should be considered. The document does not recommend any specific mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone with a dish might be able to listen in on a satellite signal without being noticed, so secret things should be locked up all the way from sender to receiver.

items.desc: Recommended; implemented on the satellite link (L).
